questions.question: A cylinder net is cut out and laid flat. It has 3 pieces: 2 equal circles and 1 rectangle. Each circle has a radius of 5 cm, and the rectangle is 12 cm wide. The long side of the rectangle must wrap exactly once around one circle. Using π = 3.14, how long is that long side?
questions.explain: The long side wraps once around the circle, so it equals the circumference: C = 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 cm. The classic trap is using the diameter (10 cm) or C = π × r instead of 2 × π × r.

questions.question: A cylinder net laid flat has 3 pieces: 2 equal circles and 1 rectangle. Each circle has a radius of 3 cm. Using π = 3.14, what is the total area of the 2 circles (the rectangle is not included)?
questions.explain: Each circle is A = π × r × r = 3.14 × 3 × 3 = 28.26 cm², and a cylinder net has two of them, so 2 × 28.26 = 56.52 cm². Two traps: using π × 2r instead of π × r × r, and counting only one circle.

questions.question: A cylinder net laid flat has 3 pieces: 2 equal circles and 1 rectangle. Each circle has a diameter of 8 cm, and the rectangle is 10 cm wide, with its length equal to the distance around one circle. Using π = 3.14, what is the area of the rectangle only?
questions.explain: The rectangle is circumference × width: C = 3.14 × 8 = 25.12 cm, so 25.12 × 10 = 251.20 cm². Watch out: 8 cm is the diameter, not the radius, and the length is never just the diameter.

questions.question: A cylinder net laid flat has 3 pieces: 2 equal circles of radius 3 cm and 1 rectangle that is 5 cm wide, whose length wraps exactly once around a circle. Using π = 3.14, what is the total area of all 3 pieces?
questions.explain: Two circles: 2 × 3.14 × 3 × 3 = 56.52 cm². Rectangle: (2 × 3.14 × 3) × 5 = 94.2 cm². Total 150.72 cm². The most common trap is making the rectangle 6 cm long (the diameter) instead of 18.84 cm (the circumference).

questions.question: A cylinder has radius r and height h. Which expression gives its total surface area, built from 2 circles plus 1 rectangle?
questions.explain: The two ends give 2πr² and the rectangle is circumference × height = 2πr × h, so the total is 2πr² + 2πrh. The trap is writing the rectangle as 2rh, which uses the diameter as its length instead of the circumference.

questions.question: A soup can for a Burnaby school food drive has a diameter of 8 cm and a height of 11 cm. A paper label wraps around the curved side only, with no overlap and nothing on the ends. Using π = 3.14, what is the area of the label?
questions.explain: The label is the rectangle of the net: circumference × height = (3.14 × 8) × 11 = 276.32 cm². Traps: treating 8 cm as the radius, and adding the two circular ends when the label covers only the side.

questions.question: Ravi draws the net of a cylindrical candle with radius 4 cm and height 9 cm. Using π = 3.14, which pair of measurements correctly describes the rectangle in his net?
questions.explain: The rectangle's length is the circumference, 2 × 3.14 × 4 = 25.12 cm, and its width is the height, 9 cm. Using 8 cm (the diameter) or 12.56 cm (π × r) for the length is the usual slip.

questions.question: A cylindrical container of trail mix has a diameter of 6 cm and a height of 10 cm. Using π = 3.14, what is its total surface area?
questions.explain: First halve the diameter: r = 3 cm. Two circles: 2 × 3.14 × 9 = 56.52 cm². Rectangle: (2 × 3.14 × 3) × 10 = 188.4 cm². Total 244.92 cm². The trap is putting the diameter 6 straight into π × r × r.

questions.question: A cylindrical rain barrel in a Surrey community garden has a diameter of 60 cm and a height of 100 cm. It is open at the top, so paint is needed on the curved side and the circular bottom only. Using π = 3.14, how much surface must be painted?
questions.explain: Side: (3.14 × 60) × 100 = 18840 cm². Bottom circle (r = 30): 3.14 × 30 × 30 = 2826 cm². Total 21666 cm². Two traps here: including a second circle for the open top, and using 60 cm as the radius.

questions.question: Maya finds the surface area of a cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. She writes: two circles = 2 × 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 157, rectangle = 10 × 12 = 120, total = 277 cm². Using π = 3.14, what went wrong?
options: The circles are wrong, because a circle's area is π × 2r, so each one is 3.14 × 10 cm².
The rectangle's length must be the circumference, 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 cm, not 10 cm.
The circles are wrong, because 10 cm across the circle is the radius to use in π × r × r.
Nothing is wrong, because the rectangle's length is the diameter, 10 cm, so 277 cm² is right.
questions.explain: Her circles are fine, but the rectangle must wrap all the way around, so its length is the circumference 31.4 cm, giving 31.4 × 12 = 376.8 cm² and a total of 533.8 cm². Using the diameter as the rectangle's length is the most common cylinder-net error.

questions.question: A wrap-around label covers the whole curved side of a cylindrical thermos with no overlap. The label has an area of 471 cm² and the thermos is 15 cm tall. Using π = 3.14, what is the total surface area of the thermos, including both circular ends?
questions.explain: Work backwards: circumference = 471 ÷ 15 = 31.4 cm, so r = 31.4 ÷ 6.28 = 5 cm, and the two ends give 2 × 3.14 × 25 = 157 cm²; 471 + 157 = 628 cm². The trap is reading 31.4 as π × r (giving r = 10) instead of 2 × π × r.

questions.question: Two cylindrical candles are wrapped completely, ends included. Candle A has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm; Candle B has radius 5 cm and height 4 cm. Using π = 3.14, which candle needs more wrapping, and by how much?
questions.explain: Candle A: 56.52 + (18.84 × 10) = 244.92 cm². Candle B: 157 + (31.4 × 4) = 282.6 cm². The difference is 37.68 cm² in favour of B. Short and wide can still beat tall and thin, but only if each rectangle uses the circumference as its length.
